A ute is not a "sporty vehicle." It is a type of pickup truck (to use  the American term) employed by Australian tradespersons. To "seep" is not to soak slowly, it is to leak liquid slowly. "Steep" would be a better answer but that of course didn't fit.

Curious as to why ALFA is not ALPHA in the Nato alphabet, I dug around and ended up on a thread (ama?) in a subreddit of air traffic controllers and pilots. ALFA, they say, is simplified because not every country or language pronounces "ph" as "f" -- and in fact, other consonant digraphs -- e.g. TH, SH, CH -- get pronounced by their first letter: "tree" for "three" and "tousand" for "thousand," because NATO is intended to be clearly pronounced in as many accents as possible, and phonetically legible with as many language backgrounds as possible. Some pilots chimed in that only the pedantic users of the Nato Alphabet say "tree" and "tousand" (and also FOW-ER for "four" apparently) but all conceded that "niner" for "nine" was nearly always used so as not to confuse it with the German "nein." 

Right on cue, a pedant joined in to correct someone who said "f" is a "softer 'p.'" sound. Pedant: "In this context, f is an unvoiced fricative with your top teeth on your lower lip. Whereas p is an unvoiced plosive with upper and lower lip. So I don't think of the phonemes as related."

Further, "The historical explanation seems to be the Greek letter phi was pronounced with a hard p plus air from the h, and so the spelling reflected that. Then Greek pronunciation changed over time to say phi with an f, but the spelling didn't change, so the old ph spelling got the association with the new f pronunciation."

Interesting to see both "legit" and "licit" in the same puzzle. Both are derived from Latin, and both stem from the language of the law. (OK, "legit" is a clipping of "legitimate," but the clipping was done in the 19th c., if not before). But beyond that, they are not etymologically related, despite the initial "l"s. And legal scholars will make a subtle distinction between that which is licit, and that which is legal, but I confess, I don't understand what it is.

In Latin, the verb form "licet"(="it is allowed") appears so often, that I tend to misspell the English word with an "e." Same with "tacit" and "tacet."

@john ezra
That 'air from the h' is the only H-sound in Greek. (Confusingly to those reading Roman alphabets, the letter H in Greek is the capital version of the vowel eta, pronounced 'ei' as in 'feign'.) It's called a rough breathing, shown as an apostrophe ' and, when there's a prefix in front, it transforms the prefix.  Examples: epi- plus ' becomes eph-. Kata- plus ' becomes kath-. And (my fave) eks plus ' becomes ekh (usually spelled in English derivatives as "ech") and pronounced with the gargly -ch of 'loch'. In each case, the transformed sound  is written as a single consonant: phi, theta, and xi.
